title: FinchBank x Redwood — enterprise change management check-in (post-rollout)
next_steps: Redwood to enable the model changelog beta feature flag for FinchBank (Console + API feed) in staging first, then production.
Redwood to share a one-pager on how pinned model versions are resolved and where the resolved model_version + changelog_url will surface in API/SDK responses.
FinchBank to provide their CAB/change-approval lead time requirements (e.g., 7/14/30 days) for model updates and deprecations.
Schedule a 30-min working session to walk through the draft release notes template and confirm what wording is acceptable for their internal change tickets.
action_items: Dev Patel — Send recap + links to upcoming changelog beta docs and the proposed change-management policy excerpt — due 2026-02-21
Paula Mendes — Confirm timeline for enrolling FinchBank in the Console “Changelog” tab beta and what account-tier gating applies — due 2026-02-24
Owen Phillips — Pull internal incident context on the confusing rollout (what changed, when, and what comms were missing) and share a customer-safe summary — due 2026-02-21
Rita Sharma — Share FinchBank CAB requirements and preferred notification channels (RSS vs email vs API polling) — due 2026-02-25
topics: What happened in the recent rollout (behavior change without a clear release note)
Difference between pinned model, resolved model version, and runtime/kernel changes
Customer-visible model changelog beta (Console tab + JSON/RSS feed)
Approval workflow and auditability (draft/in_review/published, corrections without deleting history)
Notification lead times and deprecation timelines for enterprise change management
summary: FinchBank escalated confusion from a recent model rollout where outputs shifted even though they believed they were pinned. Redwood acknowledged gaps in how model updates were communicated (missing/unclear release note and insufficient metadata surfaced in the API). Redwood walked through the upcoming customer-visible model changelog (Console + machine-readable feed) and how it will support immutable, auditable entries with a correction/supersede flow. Agreement to enroll FinchBank in the beta, starting in staging, and align on required notice periods, wording constraints, and notification format.
questions: Can FinchBank subscribe to a feed (RSS/JSON) for just the models they use, not the full catalog?
Will Redwood guarantee that pinned model_version never changes even if the serving runtime is upgraded?
How are corrections handled if a release note is wrong (do you overwrite or append)?
What retention/immutability guarantees exist for published changelog entries for audit purposes?
transcript:
Meeting: FinchBank x Redwood — enterprise change management check-in (post-rollout)
Recorded: 2026-02-20 4:00 PM PT
Duration: 47 minutes

Attendees (Redwood): Dev Patel (CSM), Owen Phillips (Escalations), Paula Mendes (Product — Rollouts)
Attendees (FinchBank): Rita Sharma (Platform Eng), Ben Wallace (SRE), Lena Ortiz (GRC/Compliance)

---

[00:00] Dev Patel: Alright, cool. Thanks everyone for making time. The goal today is basically to close the loop on last week’s, uh, confusing rollout and make sure we have a plan that fits your change-management process. I pulled Owen in since he was on the escalation thread, and Paula who owns rollouts on our side.

[00:18] Rita Sharma: Yep, thanks Dev. We appreciate it. We’re not trying to be difficult, it’s just… we have to file a change ticket for anything that changes production behavior.

[00:28] Lena Ortiz: Especially if it touches customer communications or decisioning. For us, model changes fall under “vendor-managed critical system change.”

[00:38] Dev Patel: Totally fair. And I’ll just say upfront: the way we’ve been communicating model updates has been inconsistent. That’s on us. This call is partially about what we’re rolling out to fix that.

[00:52] Ben Wallace: Can we start with a plain explanation of what happened? Because the engineering story we got internally is “we were pinned” but the outputs changed.

[01:03] Owen Phillips: Yeah, I can take first pass. So the ticket we saw—your team was using what you called “Llama 3 70B instruct” via our OpenAI-compatible route. You had the model name pinned, but you weren’t pinning the specific model version ID.

[01:20] Ben Wallace: Wait, we thought the model name is the version. Like, it’s the thing we request.

[01:26] Owen Phillips: That’s the confusing part. The request model string is an alias. Under the hood it resolves to a model version, which can move when we do a rollout unless you explicitly pin the version.

[01:39] Rita Sharma: We did set a “pinned” value in our config. I can pull it up, but it was basically the model field.

[01:46] Owen Phillips: Right. So you pinned the alias, not the resolved version. And then we did a rollout to a new version behind that alias.

[01:55] Paula Mendes: And we didn’t do a good job of providing a customer-visible release note for that change, which is what triggered the “it changed without notice” feeling. Even though it wasn’t intended to be silent.

[02:11] Dev Patel: Yeah. That’s the crux. There are two things we’re fixing: (1) the ability for you to see and pin the resolved model version easily, and (2) consistent release notes for any new version or behavior-relevant change.

[02:26] Lena Ortiz: When you say “behavior relevant,” is that subjective? Because compliance will ask me “who decided it’s relevant.”

[02:34] Paula Mendes: Good question. In the first version of our changelog system, we’re not auto-judging “quality changes” based on evals. We will publish structured notes when a model version changes: identity, compatibility, context window, quantization profile, and any known issues or policy/safety notes. For “quality deltas,” we’ll link to eval metrics where appropriate, but we won’t generate narratives from diffs yet.

[02:58] Ben Wallace: So you’re saying the release note is tied to a model version object, not like random Slack messages.

[03:03] Paula Mendes: Exactly.

[03:06] Dev Patel: Let me pause and check: does that address the “what happened” at a high level?

[03:11] Rita Sharma: Mostly. But there’s also the question of runtime changes. Our latency shifted too.

[03:17] Owen Phillips: Yep, there was also a runtime release in that week. Not sure if it’s the same day. The runtime can change kernel selection and batching behavior. That can affect latency and sometimes, rarely, tokenization edge cases.

[03:31] Ben Wallace: That’s the thing. You say “rarely,” but we saw output formatting change.

[03:36] Owen Phillips: Understood. We don’t think it was tokenizer, we think it was model version. But we’re still correlating the timeline.

[03:44] Dev Patel: We’ll send a customer-safe write-up: “model alias advanced from version A to version B; runtime updated from X to Y; release note was missing; here’s how to pin going forward.”

[03:57] Lena Ortiz: And we need the “here’s how you’ll notify us going forward.”

[04:02] Dev Patel: Yes.

[04:05] Paula Mendes: That’s what the changelog beta is meant to solve. We’re building customer-visible model changelogs generated from our model registry. The changelog entries have a workflow: draft → in_review → published.

[04:18] Ben Wallace: Who reviews it?

[04:21] Paula Mendes: Product and release engineering at minimum, and for sensitive things we pull in support readiness. The idea is: no one just ships a note ad-hoc.

[04:32] Lena Ortiz: “Sensitive” meaning what?

[04:35] Paula Mendes: Deprecations, policy-related notes, changes that might affect compliance posture, and anything that could be misconstrued. Also any note that includes a workaround.

[04:48] Rita Sharma: What about audit logs? Like, can we prove what was published at a point in time?

[04:55] Paula Mendes: Yes. Published entries are immutable in the sense that we don’t edit in place. If we need to correct something, we publish a superseding entry that references the prior entry. History stays.

[05:09] Lena Ortiz: That’s important. We’ve been burned by vendors “updating” release notes.

[05:15] Dev Patel: And the system also records who changed metadata and who approved publication.

[05:21] Ben Wallace: Will we be able to consume it in an API? We don’t want humans scraping the docs site.

[05:28] Dev Patel: That’s part of the beta: Console UI plus a machine-readable feed endpoint. We can also do RSS/Atom for the docs side.

[05:38] Rita Sharma: Can we get it scoped to the models we use? If it’s full catalog, it’s noise.

[05:44] Paula Mendes: In v1, the feed supports filtering by model_id and date ranges. I don’t want to over-promise on per-account customization immediately, but we can at least filter by model.

[05:59] Ben Wallace: Okay.

[06:00] Dev Patel: Let’s talk about the enterprise change-management angle. What notice period do you need before a model alias advances?

[06:08] Lena Ortiz: For production-impacting changes, minimum 14 days notice. For deprecations, 90 days.

[06:15] Rita Sharma: And we need a stable identifier. Like, if we pin a version, it can’t be swapped.

[06:22] Owen Phillips: If you pin the model_version, we won’t move you automatically. That’s the contract. If there’s an urgent security or severe incident, we’d still communicate, but we wouldn’t silently flip a pinned version.

[06:38] Ben Wallace: And how do we know what version we’re actually on today?

[06:42] Dev Patel: Right now, it’s harder than it should be. In the beta, we’re surfacing the resolved model_version in responses and in the Console model page. There’s a field like model_version and a changelog_url.

[06:55] Ben Wallace: In the API response itself?

[06:57] Dev Patel: Yes, via response fields and/or headers for OpenAI-compatible routes. We’ll send specifics once the endpoint is finalized.

[07:10] Rita Sharma: That’s a big deal for us. Because we can log it.

[07:13] Lena Ortiz: Exactly. If we can show “the system made a request on Feb 18 and it resolved to version XYZ,” that’s an audit artifact.

[07:25] Paula Mendes: Also in Console, rollouts will reference the changelog entry that was published at the time of the change.

[07:33] Ben Wallace: Nice.

[07:35] Dev Patel: I want to acknowledge something: the current gap is historical notes. For things that happened before the schema migration, we might not have perfect entries. But for anything going forward, it will be consistent.

[07:49] Rita Sharma: That’s okay as long as it’s explicit. “No historical data before date X.”

[07:55] Dev Patel: Yep.

[08:00] Ben Wallace: Can we go back to what actually changed? Because our app saw more refusals in a narrow category.

[08:07] Owen Phillips: That could be model policy tuning between versions. The new version had a slightly stricter safety policy config. That’s exactly the kind of thing that should have been in a release note.

[08:20] Lena Ortiz: That’s not just “nice to have,” that’s mandatory for us.

[08:24] Paula Mendes: Understood. In the schema we’re adding a “safety/policy notes” section, customer-safe language only. No internal thresholds, no vendor-only details.

[08:36] Rita Sharma: Do you include evaluation links?

[08:38] Paula Mendes: We can include links to high-level eval summaries, yes. But we’re not publishing internal prompt sets. We can link to a dashboard view that shows aggregate pass rates for categories.

[08:52] Ben Wallace: That’s fine.

[08:54] Dev Patel: On the rollout that happened: we’ll send a clear statement of whether it was (a) model version bump, (b) runtime change, or (c) both, with timestamps.

[09:06] Owen Phillips: And for the record, we think it was primarily the model version behind the alias.

[09:12] Ben Wallace: Okay.

[09:14] Dev Patel: Switching to the beta: we can enable you in staging within a few days, and then production after you sign off.

[09:23] Rita Sharma: What does “enable” mean? Feature flag in Console?

[09:26] Dev Patel: Console changelog tab, plus API feed access. Potentially the response headers too, depending on rollout.

[09:35] Ben Wallace: We don’t care about Console that much, but the feed and resolved version is huge.

[09:41] Paula Mendes: Console is still useful for humans doing incident response, but yeah, I get it.

[09:48] Lena Ortiz: Will the feed be “tamper evident”? If we download it today, will it change tomorrow?

[09:55] Paula Mendes: Entries won’t change once published. Corrections come as new entries that supersede. The feed includes stable IDs.

[10:05] Lena Ortiz: That’s acceptable.

[10:08] Ben Wallace: What about retention? We need to keep these artifacts for… seven years.

[10:14] Dev Patel: We can talk retention. Our default public changelog stays available, and internally we retain audit logs per our compliance program. For customer consumption, you can archive the feed. If you need contractual retention guarantees, we can route that through your account team.

[10:31] Rita Sharma: Alright.

[10:33] Dev Patel: Let’s also talk notification channel. Would you rather an RSS feed, a JSON feed, or email?

[10:40] Ben Wallace: JSON feed. We can poll and push into our change system.

[10:44] Lena Ortiz: We still want email for human awareness, but the system of record should be machine-readable.

[10:52] Paula Mendes: We can do both. Docs site will have RSS/Atom, API will have JSON.

[11:02] Dev Patel: Cool.

[11:05] Rita Sharma: Competing vendors—just context—Bedrock gives us a pretty clear “model version” concept, and Azure has “model deployments” that are stable. We need something comparable.

[11:18] Dev Patel: That makes sense. Our goal is similar: stable version identifiers, and a clear change feed.

[11:25] Ben Wallace: When will this be GA?

[11:27] Paula Mendes: We’re targeting a phased rollout. Beta now with a handful of enterprise customers, then GA after we harden RBAC and auditing. I don’t want to give an exact date on this call, but weeks, not quarters.

[11:44] Dev Patel: For you specifically, we can get you into beta as soon as next week in staging.

[11:51] Rita Sharma: Great.

[11:53] (crosstalk)

[11:54] Ben Wallace: Sorry, just to be clear: once we pin the version, do you still do infra-level changes that affect behavior? Like quantization.

[12:04] Owen Phillips: Quantization profile is part of the version metadata. If we changed quantization, that’s a new version. The pinned version would keep the same quantization.

[12:16] Ben Wallace: Good.

[12:18] Rita Sharma: And if capacity issues happen, you won’t silently route to a different model?

[12:24] Owen Phillips: For pinned versions, no fallback unless you configure a fallback policy. For unpinned alias, we can do compatibility fallbacks in some cases. But the default for enterprise is to be explicit.

[12:39] Dev Patel: We can review your current routing settings too. It might be worth a separate session.

[12:45] Rita Sharma: Yes, let’s do that.

[12:48] Dev Patel: Okay.

[12:50] Paula Mendes: Also, the changelog entries will include compatibility notes: tool/function calling, context window, and any constraints for dedicated/private.

[13:01] Ben Wallace: We don’t use tool calling yet, but we do care about context window because it affects truncation.

[13:07] Paula Mendes: Exactly.

[13:09] Lena Ortiz: Does the release note include “impact” in plain language? Like “you may see higher refusal rate” or “latency change”?

[13:17] Paula Mendes: Yes, we’ll have an “Impact” section. We have a style guide internally to keep it customer-safe and avoid internal jargon.

[13:27] Ben Wallace: Please avoid the “improved quality” marketing language. We need specifics.

[13:33] Dev Patel: Noted.

[13:35] Rita Sharma: Can you show an example note?

[13:38] Paula Mendes: I can’t share the internal draft live right now, but Dev can send a sanitized example template after the call.

[13:47] Dev Patel: Yep, I’ll send the template with sections: Summary, What changed, Compatibility, Performance notes, Deprecation (if any), Links.

[13:58] Ben Wallace: Perfect.

[14:00] Dev Patel: Anything else we should cover before we jump to next steps?

[14:05] Lena Ortiz: Just one more. Approvals. Who is allowed to publish? We don’t want a random engineer pushing a note.

[14:13] Paula Mendes: RBAC-wise, only specific roles can publish. Editing metadata is restricted too. Publication requires approver role. We can share the policy language.

[14:26] Lena Ortiz: Good.

[14:28] Ben Wallace: And for urgent hotfixes, how do you communicate?

[14:32] Dev Patel: There’s an emergency path: we can publish quickly but still log approvals and follow up with a full note. And we’d also use your agreed channel.

[14:43] Rita Sharma: Okay.

[14:45] Dev Patel: Alright, let’s do a recap.

[14:48] Dev Patel: One, Owen will send a customer-safe summary of last week’s incident: what changed, timestamps, and the gap in release note. Two, we’ll enroll FinchBank in the changelog beta in staging first—Console tab plus API/feed access. Three, I’ll send a template release note and the “pinning/resolved version” explanation. Four, Rita you’ll send us CAB notice period requirements and preferred channels.

[15:12] Rita Sharma: Yes.

[15:14] Ben Wallace: And we’ll want a short working session on routing/pinning best practices.

[15:18] Dev Patel: Yep, we’ll schedule that.

[15:21] Lena Ortiz: Thanks. This is moving in the right direction.

[15:24] Dev Patel: Thanks all. I’ll send the email recap today or tomorrow morning.

---

(Transcript continues with scheduling and minor Q&A; primary decisions and action items captured above.)
